facts.text: Training first learns an asymmetric tokenizer: an action-only one-dimensional convolutional encoder compresses action chunks, while a recurrent GRU decoder reconstructs actions using both the latent chunk and tactile or force information. TactAR supplies augmented-reality contact feedback for demonstration collection. Across peeling, wiping, and bimanual lifting, RDP improves task-specific scores over open-loop Diffusion Policy. Under post-contact peeling disturbances, GelSight RDP scores 0.80 versus 0.15 for tactile-input Diffusion Policy, distinguishing reactive architecture from tactile input alone. The slow planner runs at 12 Hz and the decoder at 24 Hz, constrained by GelSight's 25-frame-per-second stream; higher-rate operation remains untested. Trajectories referenced to each chunk's last observation frame and latency-matched execution support smooth transitions.

It instead trains Diffusion Policy jointly on real and simulated demonstrations, using RGB images and robot proprioception to predict action sequences. For task-aware Panda simulation, each task uses 100 source demonstrations to generate 10,000 demonstrations. Each task-aware GR-1 simulation task uses ten source demonstrations to generate 1,000 trajectories.

facts.location: PDF page 4, Section IV-A, Real-World Domains; PDF page 6, Section IV-D, Training and Evaluation Protocol.

A GR-1 humanoid learns CupPnP, MilkPnP, and pouring a ping-pong ball from a cup into a bowl from 20 real demonstrations per task. Trained policies are deployed on these real tasks and evaluated by trial success rate.

facts.text: Table I reports average real-world success rates of 45.3% for real-only training, 81.1% for real plus task-aware digital cousins, 76.8% for real plus prior simulation, and 83.2% for real plus both simulation sources. These values are the table's reported aggregate success rates, not relative improvement percentages or individual-task measurements.

facts.location: PDF page 7, Section V-B, Generalization Beyond Real Demonstrations; PDF page 8, Table II and continuation of Section V-B.
facts.text: For unseen objects, real-plus-digital-cousin training raises success from 33% to 50% on Panda CounterToSinkPnP and from 10% to 80% on GR-1 CupPnP. For unseen positions, the corresponding changes are 11% to 28% and 43% to 100%. The position control removes central-workspace placements from real training demonstrations but retains uniformly distributed simulation placements; evaluation then places objects in the withheld center.

facts.location: PDF page 8, Figure 5 and Section V-D, Key Elements of Effective Co-Training; PDF page 9, continuation of the co-training-ratio discussion.
facts.text: The CupPnP sampling-ratio experiment fixes the datasets at 20 real demonstrations and 1,000 task-aware simulation demonstrations. Figure 5 shows 85% success with 50% simulation sampling, 95% success with either 90% or 99% simulation sampling, and 60% success at 99.9% simulation sampling. Thus the mixture weight matters independently of stored dataset size, and increasing simulation sampling is not uniformly beneficial.

facts.location: PDF page 9, Section V-D, Camera alignment is critical for successful co-training with task-aware digital cousin data, and Figure 6.
facts.text: Changing from approximately aligned to default unaligned simulation-camera views lowers real-plus-digital-cousin success from 67% to 56% on Panda CounterToSinkPnP and from 95% to 70% on GR-1 CupPnP. Alignment remains approximate: the real humanoid camera has fisheye distortion that is not modeled in the aligned simulation camera. The experiment therefore supports useful approximate alignment rather than a requirement for identical cameras.

facts.location: PDF page 9, Section VI, Limitations.
facts.text: Most evaluated tasks are pick-and-place variants. High-precision insertion and longer-horizon manipulation are left for future study, and the learned policies are not uniformly successful. questions: Which properties must digital cousins preserve, and which simulation-to-real mismatches remain permissible?
How much do prior simulation and task-aware digital cousins each contribute beyond real-only training?

versions.A: Joint training on real and simulated demonstrations can improve manipulation policies without exact scene replication. This study co-trains Diffusion Policy with task-aware digital cousins, prior simulation data, or both. Digital cousins preserve the robot, action space, task goal, success criteria, and object and fixture categories, while allowing different object instances and physical and visual properties. Across six real-world tasks on Panda and GR-1 robots, reported average success rises from 45.3% with real-only training to 81.1% with digital cousins, 76.8% with prior simulation, and 83.2% with both. Generated demonstrations broaden training coverage, and evaluations also test unseen objects and positions. Transfer depends on simulation sampling probability and approximate camera alignment, without requiring identical camera models. Prior Panda trajectories are re-rendered to approximately align camera poses, qualifying the use of prior simulation data.
versions.B: Learning real-robot manipulation from limited demonstrations can benefit from simulation without exact replication of the real scene. This study co-trains Diffusion Policy on real trajectories and either task-aware digital cousins, prior simulation data, or both. Digital cousins preserve robot, action space, task goals, and object and fixture categories; generated trajectories broaden training coverage. Across six tasks on Panda and GR-1 robots, the reported average success rate rises from 45.3% with real data to 83.2% with both simulation sources. Experiments also test unseen objects and positions. Transfer quality depends on simulation sampling ratios and approximate camera alignment, without requiring identical camera models.
versions.C: Real-robot imitation learning faces costly demonstrations and simulation-to-real mismatch. This study co-trains Diffusion Policy on real demonstrations and task-aware digital cousins, independently developed simulation data, or both. Digital cousins preserve embodiment, action space, task goals and success criteria, and object and fixture categories, without requiring identical object instances or physical and visual properties. Task-aware demonstrations are generated by transforming and recombining object-centered trajectory segments. Across six real-world tasks on Panda and GR-1 robots, reported average success rates are 45.3% with real-only training, 81.1% with added digital cousins, 76.8% with added prior simulation, and 83.2% with both sources. Transfer depends on simulation sampling probability, not just dataset size, and benefits from approximate camera alignment despite mismatched camera models. Prior Panda data also undergo camera re-rendering; the findings therefore do not establish transfer from entirely unmodified simulation data.
versions.D: Co-training Diffusion Policy supplements scarce real demonstrations with task-aware digital cousins, prior simulation data, or both. Digital cousins preserve the robot, action space, task goals and success criteria, and object and fixture categories, but allow different object instances and physical and visual properties. Across six tasks on Panda and GR-1, average real-world success rises from 45.3% with real-only training to 81.1% with digital cousins, 76.8% with prior simulation, and 83.2% with both. questions: How do the learned barrier and rollout resampling address different failures of short-horizon sampling-based MPC?
What short-horizon and CPU evidence supports the method, and why does it not establish a general safety guarantee?

versions.A: Sampling-based MPC can satisfy predicted constraints yet enter states that become unsafe after its horizon. Neural Shield VIMPC combines a learned discrete-time policy barrier with resampling-based rollouts. The barrier approximates a policy's worst future constraint value; rollout resampling replaces unsafe prefixes with safe ones. In drone simulations using 500 sampled trajectories, NS-MPPI avoided crashes even at a ten-step horizon. On AutoRally, a 12 m/s target, 15-step horizon and 30 trajectories yielded a 0.04 crash rate at 73.64 Hz on a CPU, compared with 0.46 for S-MPPI. These results concern an unverified barrier approximation, not a general safety guarantee.
versions.B: Short-horizon sampling-based MPC can miss later hazards and waste samples whose violation penalties drive their weights toward zero. Neural Shield VIMPC addresses these failures separately: a learned approximation of a policy's worst future constraint value brings post-horizon information into a discrete-time barrier descent constraint, while rollout resampling replaces unsafe states and control prefixes with safe counterparts when available. With 500 sampled trajectories, NS-MPPI alone among tested controllers had zero Drone crashes across evaluated horizons, including ten steps. At a 12 m/s AutoRally target speed, 15-step horizon and 30 trajectories per optimization iteration, its crash rate was 0.04 versus S-MPPI's 0.46, with CPU control at 73.64 Hz. These empirical improvements do not establish a safety guarantee: the learned barrier is unverified, and averaging constraint-satisfying controls can violate nonconvex safety constraints.
versions.C: Sampling-based MPC can satisfy predicted constraints yet become unsafe beyond its horizon, while barrier penalties can leave most rollouts with negligible importance weights. Neural Shield VIMPC addresses these failures through a learned discrete-time policy barrier and rollout resampling. The barrier approximates a policy's worst future constraint value to anticipate hazards beyond the horizon; resampling replaces unsafe states and control prefixes with safe counterparts when available, retaining control suffixes. With 500 trajectories, NS-MPPI had no crashes across tested Drone horizons, including ten steps. On AutoRally, a 12 m/s target speed, 15-step horizon and 30 trajectories per iteration yielded a crash rate of 0.04 versus S-MPPI's 0.46, at 73.64 Hz on a CPU. These findings support empirical safety, not a general guarantee: the barrier is unverified, and averaging feasible controls can violate nonconvex safety constraints.
versions.D: Neural Shield VIMPC addresses two sampling-based MPC failures: a learned discrete-time policy barrier estimates worst future constraint values beyond the horizon, while rollout resampling replaces unsafe prefixes with available safe ones to reduce sample waste. With 500 trajectories, NS-MPPI had zero drone crashes at a ten-step horizon. On AutoRally, a 12 m/s target, 15-step horizon and 30 trajectories per iteration yielded a 0.04 crash rate versus S-MPPI's 0.46, at 73.64 Hz on a CPU. cases.contribution: ArticuBot learns a hierarchical, point-cloud-based opening policy from simulated demonstrations, using weighted displacement subgoals and a conditioned diffusion controller for zero-shot transfer to unseen articulated objects and two robot embodiments.

facts.location: PDF page 2, Section I; PDF page 3, Section III
facts.text: The task is to open articulated objects with a parallel-jaw gripper despite differences in object geometry and articulation. Objects must have handles graspable from the fully closed state. Deployment assumes a target-object name for open-vocabulary segmentation into object-only point clouds; the learned policy does not receive articulation parameters. Simulation generation does require object assets with handle annotations.

facts.location: PDF pages 3-5, Section IV-A
facts.text: Simulation demonstrations combine handle-grasp sampling, collision-free approach planning and opening actions computed from ground-truth articulation. Failed or insufficient openings are discarded; retained candidates are ranked by grasp stability and approach-path length. Object pose, size and the robot's initial configuration are randomized, so the data-generation stage uses information unavailable to the deployed policy.

facts.location: PDF page 10, Section VI-A, paragraphs beginning 'For robust sim2real transfer'
facts.text: The final real-transfer training dataset combines 42.3k simulation trajectories and 4.7 million observation-action pairs over 322 objects. Depth augmentations simulate edge artifacts and missing pixels, and camera poses are randomized near real-camera placements. This dataset trains one weighted-displacement high-level policy; the low-level policy is transferred without training on these depth augmentations.

facts.location: PDF page 5, Section IV-B, 'High-Level Policy'; PDF pages 6-7, Section IV-B, 'Low-level Policy'; PDF page 7, Section IV-C
facts.text: The hierarchy predicts end-effector subgoals for grasping a handle and completing the opening. A modified 3D diffusion policy conditions on the current object point cloud, current end-effector state and predicted subgoal to output delta translation, rotation and finger movement. It learns task actions rather than merely reaching the subgoal. Both levels are rerun from current observations during execution.

facts.location: PDF page 6, Section IV-B, weighted displacement model, equations (3)-(4)
facts.text: The high-level weighted displacement model represents a gripper subgoal by four 3D landmarks: the hand root, both fingers and the closed-grasp center. PointNet++ predicts scene-point offsets to these landmarks and a weight per scene point. The final landmark predictions are weighted averages of each scene point plus its offset, grounding pose prediction in observed geometry rather than averaging orientation vectors.

facts.location: PDF page 7, Section V-A and Figure 3; PDF page 8, Section V-B
